paragraphs: Navigation agents that follow language instructions can struggle in environments unlike their training data. One adaptation strategy makes their action predictions more confident, but confidence alone can reinforce mistakes. ATENA addresses this problem by using episodic feedback about uncertain navigation outcomes to guide learning during deployment.

The framework increases certainty after successful episodes and decreases it after failed ones. Its mixture entropy objective combines the agent’s action distribution with a hypothetical distribution that treats its selected action as optimal. This combination controls both confidence and action preference. A complementary self-active learning strategy lets the agent assess navigation outcomes using confident predictions, keeping adaptation active throughout the process.

Evaluations on REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE show improvements over the compared baselines across multiple settings involving distribution shifts. The findings support adapting confidence according to navigation outcomes rather than simply increasing it. Episodic feedback is an explicit part of the proposed interaction framework, alongside the agent’s ability to evaluate some outcomes itself.
neurips-2025-active-test-time-vision-lan.tldr: ATENA adapts navigation agents during deployment by using episode outcomes to adjust confidence and action choices.

paragraphs: Federated continual learning combines two difficulties: clients learn from different data, and new tasks keep arriving over time. Sharing task-specific prompts can transfer knowledge between clients, but the paper identifies class-level inconsistencies that make this communication less reliable. These inconsistencies can create conflicts between new prompts and interfere with older ones.

C²Prompt addresses two sources of conflict. First, examples from the same class can have different distributions across clients, weakening agreement about what that class represents. A local class distribution compensation mechanism reduces those disparities. Second, prompts can mix knowledge relevant to different classes. A class-aware aggregation scheme selectively strengthens the combination of class-relevant knowledge to reduce that confusion.

The approach therefore changes how clients reconcile and combine prompt knowledge, explicitly accounting for classes during communication. Experiments on multiple federated continual learning benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance. These results support the paper’s argument that improving class-level coherence can help address forgetting both across distributed clients and across successive tasks.
neurips-2025-c-2-prompt-class-aware-clie.tldr: C²Prompt improves federated continual learning by reducing class-level conflicts when clients share and aggregate prompts.

paragraphs: Models for designing cyclic peptides need examples of how these molecules interact with protein receptors, but available data are scarce. CPSea addresses that bottleneck with 2.71 million cyclic peptide–receptor complexes assembled by systematically mining the AlphaFold Database. The motivation is to support design models for peptides with favorable binding and resistance to protein-degrading enzymes.

The construction pipeline extracts compact protein domains, identifies possible cyclization sites using distances between beta-carbon atoms, and applies several filtering stages. These filters target structural fidelity and compatibility with binding. A central idea is to use interactions within a protein chain to simulate interactions between separate chains, expanding the pool of usable structural examples.

Compared with experimental cyclic peptide data, CPSea has similar distributions on the reported structural fidelity and wet-lab compatibility metrics. That comparison supports the dataset’s relevance without making its mined complexes experimental observations. The authors describe it as the largest such dataset to their knowledge and argue that its scale enables end-to-end model training.
neurips-2025-cpsea-large-scale-cyclic-pe.tldr: CPSea mines protein structures to provide 2.71 million cyclic peptide–receptor complexes for training peptide design models.

paragraphs: Robot policies need to respond to objectives that arise during deployment. Common approaches such as goal-conditioning train the policy with anticipated objectives in mind. DynaGuide introduces a separate source of guidance: an external dynamics model that steers a diffusion policy while it denoises its proposed behavior.

Separating this guidance from the base policy allows the method to work with existing pretrained diffusion policies. The paper describes several benefits of this arrangement, including steering toward multiple objectives, strengthening behaviors that are underrepresented in the base policy, and remaining robust when objectives are low quality. The policy supplies its learned behavior, while the separate model supplies steering information.

In simulated and real experiments, DynaGuide achieves 70% average steering success on a set of articulated CALVIN tasks. With low-quality objectives, it outperforms goal-conditioning by 5.4 times. The authors also steer an off-the-shelf real robot policy toward preferred objects and demonstrate novel behavior. These findings show how external guidance can expand the uses of an already trained policy.
neurips-2025-dynaguide-steering-diffusio.tldr: DynaGuide uses a separate dynamics model to steer pretrained diffusion policies toward deployment-time objectives.

paragraphs: First-person video reasoning requires understanding someone who is largely invisible: the person behind the camera. Their intentions and interactions shape what happens on screen. EgoThinker targets this challenge by training multimodal language models to reason about interactions across both space and time, beyond recognizing visible events.

The framework introduces EgoRe-5M, a question-answering dataset constructed from 13 million diverse egocentric video clips. Its multi-minute segments include detailed reasoning rationales and dense annotations connecting hands with objects. Training follows two stages: supervised fine-tuning develops the reasoning skills, and reinforcement fine-tuning further improves the ability to locate relevant interactions in space and time.

Experiments report stronger performance than existing methods across multiple egocentric benchmarks, together with substantial gains in fine-grained localization. The contribution connects explanation supervision with detailed visual grounding: the model learns reasoning traces alongside evidence about where and when interactions occur. The reported results support this combination as a way to improve understanding of first-person activities and their hidden agent.
neurips-2025-egothinker-unveiling-egocen.tldr: EgoThinker combines detailed first-person video supervision with two-stage training to improve reasoning and interaction localization.

paragraphs: Generating convincing first-person video requires handling a moving viewpoint, varied actions, and diverse scenes together. EgoVid-5M addresses the data needs of this task with more than five million egocentric video clips. The dataset is specifically curated for generation, where coherent movement and action control are central concerns.

Each clip is enriched with action information at two levels: high-level text descriptions and fine-grained kinematic control annotations. These provide complementary descriptions of what is happening and how movement unfolds. A data cleansing pipeline checks frame consistency, action coherence, and motion smoothness under first-person viewing conditions, aiming to make the collected material usable for generation research.

The paper also introduces EgoDreamer, which generates egocentric videos using action descriptions and kinematic signals simultaneously. Together, the dataset and generator connect verbal intent with detailed motion control. The authors position this work as infrastructure for first-person world simulation, with potential applications in virtual reality, augmented reality, and gaming, and state plans to release the annotations and cleansing metadata.
neurips-2025-egovid-5m-a-large-scale-vid.tldr: EgoVid-5M supplies over five million annotated first-person clips, alongside a generator controlled by text and motion signals.

paragraphs: Vision-based autonomous driving models often learn visual features through labeled supervision. This paper argues that such supervision restricts the generality of the resulting driving systems. E³AD explores an additional training signal: representations of human driving cognition obtained through a general EEG large model.

The authors collect a cognitive dataset and use comparative, or contrastive, learning between the EEG model and the driving system’s visual feature extractor. The intended result is a visual representation informed by latent human driving cognition, which can improve end-to-end planning. They investigate both methods for incorporating this information and possible mechanisms behind the resulting gains.

Evaluations use popular driving models on public autonomous driving datasets, with both open-loop and closed-loop tests. The reported results show significant planning improvements over the baseline models. Ablation studies support contributions from the cognitive information and the comparative learning process. The paper frames this as an initial attempt to incorporate embodied cognitive data into driving systems, with evidence for improving planning in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2025-embodied-cognition-augmente.tldr: E³AD uses contrastive learning with EEG-derived representations of human driving cognition to improve autonomous driving planning.

paragraphs: A diffusion model’s generation quality depends partly on where its sampling steps fall along the noise-removal process. This paper proposes choosing those points according to entropy, so that each contributes an equal amount of information to the final output. The resulting entropic time replaces uniform spacing in the original time coordinate.

The authors prove that this reparameterization is independent of the initial choice of time. They also provide a tractable exact formula for estimating entropic time from a trained model’s training loss without substantial overhead. Alongside this construction, they introduce a rescaled version motivated by optimality results.

Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and ImageNet show substantial inference improvements from the entropic schedules. For pretrained EDM2 models, rescaled entropic time improves image quality measured by FID and FD-DINO without increasing the number of function evaluations. The gains are greater when only a few evaluations are used. These findings show that allocating existing sampling steps more effectively can improve generation without spending more model evaluations.
neurips-2025-entropic-time-schedulers-fo.tldr: Entropy-based sampling schedules improve diffusion generation by reallocating existing evaluation steps according to information contribution.

paragraphs: In-context compositional learning asks a model to infer rules from examples and apply them to a new problem. The paper argues that standard Transformers have limited built-in structure for this task. Its proposed attention reformulation uses sparse coding to make combinations of basic components more explicit.

The method interprets attention through two learned dictionaries. An encoding dictionary turns the input into coefficients describing its composition, and sparsity encourages that description to use relatively few components. A decoding dictionary then produces the output by combining its elements according to those coefficients. For compositional generalization, the method also estimates a target problem’s coefficients as a linear combination of coefficients from context examples.

Experiments on S-RAVEN and RAVEN demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. On certain compositional generalization tasks, it preserves performance where standard Transformers fail. The result supports adding structure to how attention represents and reuses combinations: context examples contribute compositional representations that can help construct the representation needed for a new target.
neurips-2025-in-context-compositional-le.tldr: A sparse-coding reformulation of attention helps Transformers infer and reuse compositional rules from context examples.

paragraphs: Red-teaming language models requires methods that expose failures in their safeguards. LARGO studies whether gradient-based optimization can produce effective, fluent jailbreak prompts. Its starting point is that optimizing discrete words is difficult, while a model’s continuous internal representations provide a different space in which to search.

The method first optimizes an adversarial latent vector, then recursively uses the same language model to decode that vector into natural language. This latent self-reflection process connects an internally optimized representation with a readable prompt. The authors report that the resulting attacks are fast, effective, transferable, and fluent, with stealthy wording.

On benchmarks including AdvBench and JailbreakBench, the paper reports a 44-point attack success rate advantage over leading techniques, including AutoDAN. The finding supports continuous latent optimization as a powerful alternative to approaches that use language models as prompt-writing optimizers. Its significance for evaluation is that natural-looking attack text can arise from optimization of model internals, exposing vulnerabilities through a different route.
neurips-2025-largo-latent-adversarial-re.tldr: LARGO turns optimized internal representations into fluent jailbreak prompts, reporting strong attack performance on standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: Restoring ultra-high-definition images requires preserving detail while keeping computation manageable. Processing compressed VAE representations helps with efficiency, but the paper argues that the usual Gaussian constraint can discard degradation-sensitive, high-frequency information. Latent Harmony redesigns this representation and its reconstruction process to better support restoration.

The first stage trains LH-VAE with visual semantic constraints and progressively perturbed degradations to strengthen semantic robustness. It also introduces latent equivariance to improve high-frequency reconstruction. The second stage jointly trains the refined VAE and a restoration model. Separate low-rank adaptation modules serve different purposes: the encoder emphasizes extraction of authentic details, while the decoder emphasizes perceptually appealing textures.

Alternating optimization and selective gradient propagation help preserve the pretrained latent structure during this second stage. At inference, an adjustable parameter controls the balance between reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality. Experiments across UHD and standard-resolution settings report superior restoration performance while balancing these objectives efficiently. The framework makes that balance an explicit, adjustable part of the restoration system.
neurips-2025-latent-harmony-synergistic-.tldr: Latent Harmony redesigns VAE-based restoration to preserve fine detail and provide adjustable control over fidelity and perceptual quality.

paragraphs: Selective unlearning must suppress targeted knowledge while preserving a language model’s broader usefulness. LUNAR approaches this through internal representations: it redirects activations associated with the targeted data toward regions that express inability to answer. The method is grounded in the Linear Representation Hypothesis.

The authors show that effective activation redirection does not require contrastive features. They also restrict parameter updates to a single down-projection matrix, reporting a 20-fold efficiency improvement and enhanced robustness. This narrow update design accompanies controllability at inference time and coherent, contextually appropriate responses after unlearning.

Across several base models, LUNAR reports improvements of 2.9 to 11.7 times in Deviation Score, which combines unlearning efficacy with retained model utility. The paper also demonstrates robustness against white-box adversarial attacks and support for sequential unlearning requests. These findings position representation redirection as a way to manage the trade-off between suppressing targeted knowledge and maintaining useful behavior, with the reported score measuring both goals together.
neurips-2025-llm-unlearning-via-neural-a.tldr: LUNAR redirects targeted internal activations toward inability-to-answer responses while preserving utility through a narrowly scoped parameter update.

paragraphs: Improving a black-box language model through ordinary parameter adaptation is infeasible when its weights are inaccessible. Matryoshka Pilot addresses this by training a smaller, accessible language model to guide the larger generator. The controller breaks complex tasks into intermediate outputs and supplies guidance through prompts.

The framework treats the black-box generator as an environment and the controller as a policy acting within it. During iterative interaction, M-Pilot learns to steer the generator’s outputs toward preferences. This makes guidance a learned, multi-turn process: the controller improves how it directs intermediate generation while working through the larger task.

Evaluations across diverse tasks report improved capabilities on complex problems with long horizons. The findings support a division of labor in which the large model provides generation and the lightweight model learns how to direct it. The practical contribution is an adaptation route that works through interaction with the black-box system, making controllable multi-turn generation possible without needing access to that generator’s parameters.
neurips-2025-matryoshka-pilot-learning-t.tldr: M-Pilot trains a lightweight language-model controller to improve black-box generators through learned, multi-turn prompt guidance.

paragraphs: Learning new classes can shift a pretrained model’s parameters and weaken knowledge useful for earlier tasks. This paper views that drift as harmful noise, while observing that carefully chosen noise can also help. Suppressing features weakly related to the current task may leave more room for future learning.

Mixture of Noise, or MiN, learns task-specific noise from high-dimensional features, guided by information theory. It then dynamically adjusts weights that combine noise learned for different tasks. The resulting mixture is inserted into intermediate features to mask responses from inefficient patterns. The aim is to reduce the loss of generalization that can accompany adaptation to new classes.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets report state-of-the-art performance in most incremental settings, with especially strong results in 50-step settings. These findings support treating noise as something that can be learned and combined for a useful purpose. The contribution is a mechanism for shaping feature use over successive tasks, using beneficial noise to help preserve the value of pretraining.
neurips-2025-mixture-of-noise-for-pre-tr.tldr: MiN learns and mixes task-specific noise to suppress inefficient feature responses and improve class-incremental learning.

paragraphs: Estimating mutual information requires a model of statistical dependence that is expressive enough for the data. The paper identifies a tension between two common approaches. Highly flexible estimators, including neural networks, need large amounts of data, while simpler approaches such as Gaussian copulas can miss complex distributions.

The proposed method draws on vector copula theory to interpolate between these extremes. Its purpose is to create a more balanced relationship between model complexity and representational capacity. This makes the choice of estimator structure central to the contribution: enough flexibility is needed to capture complicated dependence, but greater flexibility also brings data demands.

Experiments use state-of-the-art synthetic benchmarks and real-world data spanning diverse modalities, and the authors report advantages for the proposed estimator. These results support the value of an intermediate approach between very flexible neural estimators and restrictive models. The paper’s stated contribution is a principled way to navigate that trade-off, supported by evaluations across both constructed and real datasets.
neurips-2025-neural-mutual-information-e.tldr: A vector-copula-based estimator balances flexibility and complexity to improve mutual information estimation across diverse datasets.

paragraphs: Existing infinite-width theory predicts a troubling choice for networks with He initialization and a global learning rate: instability at large rates or vanishing feature learning at stable ones. Practical networks can instead train stably and keep learning features. This paper argues that finite width does not fully explain the discrepancy.

Under cross-entropy loss, the authors separate the supposedly unstable region into catastrophic instability and controlled divergence. In the latter, logits diverge while gradients and activations remain stable. At large learning rates near this region’s edge, they establish an infinite-width limit in which features continue evolving throughout all hidden layers.

Experiments across optimizers, architectures, and data modalities support controlled divergence under cross-entropy, but not under mean squared error. Empirical evidence also suggests that width scaling helps predict maximal stable learning-rate exponents, informing choices of optimal exponents. The result refines what instability means in this setting and clarifies both the usefulness and limitations of recently proposed layerwise learning-rate scalings.
neurips-2025-on-the-surprising-effective.tldr: A controlled-divergence regime under cross-entropy explains how wide networks can use large learning rates while continuing to learn features.

paragraphs: Transformers produce contextual representations for individual tokens, but many downstream tasks need a single fixed-size vector. Pooling performs that conversion. This paper examines how the pooling choice affects a model’s capabilities, addressing an architectural step that has received less attention than the attention mechanism itself.

The authors develop a theoretical framework with closed-form bounds on representational capacity and the ability to distinguish similar inputs. They extend the analysis across different attention formulations, showing that the bounds apply to diverse architectural variants. This connects pooling directly to what information a complete Transformer-based model can represent and separate.

Experiments cover computer vision, language processing, and time-series analysis, including tasks needing global and local context. The results reveal consistent patterns in how pooling affects accuracy, sensitivity, and optimization. Together, the theory and experiments support choosing pooling mechanisms according to task needs. The central implication is that aggregating token representations is a consequential design decision, with effects that extend beyond the quality of attention alone.
neurips-2025-pool-me-wisely-on-the-effec.tldr: Theoretical bounds and cross-modal experiments show how pooling choices shape Transformer capacity, sensitivity, and training behavior.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks implant triggers that redirect a language model’s behavior. RepGuard targets the unreliable internal features supporting those attacks, aiming to separate them from useful semantic information. Its defense is designed to operate without depending on knowledge of particular trigger patterns.

The method first locates suspicious features using two perspectives: local consistency and deviations measured across individual samples. It then generates adaptive masks that isolate shortcut features targeted by the backdoor, decomposing hidden representations into independent spaces. A multi-objective training framework combines this separation with preservation of task-relevant semantics.

Tests cover Target Refusal and Jailbreak tasks under four attack types. RepGuard reduces attack success on poisoned data by nearly 80% on average while keeping performance on clean data near its original level. These results support the idea that separating suspicious representation components can mitigate backdoors without sacrificing much ordinary task performance in the evaluated settings. The defense’s focus is the model’s reliance on abnormal features, giving it a mechanism that is not tied to a specific trigger.
neurips-2025-repguard-adaptive-feature-d.tldr: RepGuard separates suspicious internal features from useful semantics, reducing backdoor attack success while largely preserving clean-data performance.

paragraphs: Simpson’s paradox creates conflicting associations when data are viewed in aggregate or through finer-grained conditioning. The paper first revisits how often it occurs using an unbiased data generation process. This reaffirms that the paradox cannot simply be dismissed as a consequence of deficient data collection.

The proposed resolution assumes a minimal common cause, also described as a screening variable, for the random variables involved. This cause need not be observed. Within the authors’ approach, conditioning on it establishes the correct association between events, and that association agrees with the fine-grained conditioning option in the original paradox.

The result applies to discrete binary variables and to continuous settings modeled with Gaussian variables. Minimality matters: with a non-minimal common cause, resolution remains possible but requires detailed knowledge of that cause. The paper’s contribution is therefore a conditional principle for deciding between conflicting associations, grounded in a specified common-cause assumption. Examples illustrate how this principle can guide probabilistic inference and the recommendations drawn from it.
neurips-2025-resolution-of-simpson-s-par.tldr: Assuming a minimal common cause resolves Simpson’s paradox in the studied binary and Gaussian settings by favoring the conditioned association.

paragraphs: Several small decision trees can predict almost equally well while using different structures. A Rashomon set collects these alternatives, allowing users to examine explanations, variable importance, simplicity, or stakeholder preferences. Finding even one optimal tree is NP-hard, which makes enumerating a collection of strong alternatives difficult.

SORTD improves this process by producing trees in order of their objective value. This ordering gives the framework anytime behavior: useful results become available as enumeration progresses. Users can explore high-performing alternatives without requiring every preference, such as fairness, to be encoded in the original optimization objective.

Experiments report runtime reductions of up to two orders of magnitude relative to the state of the art. The framework supports any separable, totally ordered objective for building the set, and other separable, partially ordered objectives for later evaluation. These advances make it more practical to inspect competing interpretable models and choose among them using criteria that go beyond the objective that generated the set.
neurips-2025-sorted-rashomon-sets-of-spa.tldr: SORTD efficiently enumerates similarly performing sparse decision trees in objective order, making useful alternatives available throughout the search.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input falls outside the kinds of data a model learned from. Spurious correlations can undermine that judgment by making unreliable features appear informative. SPROD addresses this problem by refining class prototypes, the representations used to summarize known classes.

The method operates after training and is designed to reduce prototype bias from unknown spurious features. It requires neither additional data nor hyperparameter tuning. The authors describe it as broadly applicable across model backbones and detection settings, making prototype refinement the main intervention rather than collecting new examples or adjusting a separate tuning process.

The evaluation compares methods on challenging datasets including CelebA, Waterbirds, UrbanCars, Spurious Imagenet, and the newly introduced Animals MetaCoCo. SPROD reports average improvements of 4.8% in AUROC and 9.4% in FPR@95 over the second-best method. These results support correcting the influence of misleading features in class summaries as a practical way to improve detection reliability under the benchmarked spurious correlations.
neurips-2025-spurious-aware-prototype-re.tldr: SPROD refines class prototypes after training to improve out-of-distribution detection under unknown spurious correlations.

paragraphs: Networks solving modular addition can have different-looking neuron representations, which prior work interpreted as different algorithms. This paper proposes that those solutions instead share a common abstract algorithm. It studies the question at several levels, from individual neurons to neuron clusters and whole networks.

The authors identify this algorithm as an approximate Chinese Remainder Theorem and report that multilayer perceptrons and Transformers universally implement it in their analysis of modular addition. They introduce approximate cosets and show that neuron activations occur exclusively on these structures. This links local activation patterns to a shared description of the network’s overall computation.

The theory also covers deep networks. For networks with trainable embeddings or more than one hidden layer, it predicts universally learned solutions using only O(log n) features, a prediction confirmed empirically. The contribution is a theory-backed account of multilayer modular addition that connects apparently different representations. Extension to group multiplication beyond modular addition is presented as a testable universality hypothesis.
neurips-2025-uncovering-a-universal-abst.tldr: The paper identifies an approximate Chinese Remainder Theorem algorithm underlying neural modular addition and explains its compact feature requirements.

paragraphs: Visual foundation models can struggle when deployment data differ from pretraining data and labels are scarce. VESSA adapts these models using short, object-centered videos with multiple views, requiring no annotations. Different frames provide observations of the same object under varied capture conditions.

Training uses self-distillation, with careful tuning of prediction heads and parameter-efficient adaptation. The paper emphasizes that these design choices are critical: without them, the model can quickly forget its pretrained knowledge and degrade. Multi-view observations are particularly beneficial, helping the adapted representation become more robust to changes in how an object is captured.

Experiments with three visual foundation models on two datasets show consistent downstream classification improvements over the original models and previous adaptation methods. The findings support using unlabeled object videos as a source of domain adaptation signals. They also show why the adaptation procedure matters: preserving pretrained knowledge while learning from new views is central to making continued self-supervised training effective for these vision encoders.
neurips-2025-vessa-video-based-object-ce.tldr: VESSA adapts visual foundation models with unlabeled multi-view object videos while carefully controlling updates to preserve pretrained knowledge.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks are often analyzed by which graphs they can distinguish. This paper argues that such expressivity analysis gives an incomplete account of practical performance. Its binary distinction between possible and impossible misses how difficult a task can be for a particular architecture.

The authors introduce Message Passing Complexity, a continuous measure of the difficulty of solving a task through message passing. It captures practical obstacles such as over-squashing while retaining theoretical impossibility results from expressivity analysis. The paper also argues that most real-world tasks rarely need expressivity beyond the basic Weisfeiler–Leman test, questioning the value of pursuing higher expressivity alone.

Validation on fundamental graph neural network tasks shows that the measure’s theoretical predictions correlate with empirical performance and explain architectural successes and failures. This supports evaluating how effectively information can support a task within an architecture, alongside asking whether the task is theoretically distinguishable. The proposed framework aims to make theoretical analysis more informative for understanding and designing practical graph models.
neurips-2025-what-expressivity-theory-mi.tldr: Message Passing Complexity measures task difficulty for graph neural networks beyond the binary distinctions of expressivity theory.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization trains language models from preferred and rejected responses without learning a separate reward model. This paper asks which properties of those examples matter most. Its central finding is that chosen-response quality dominates optimization, while rejected-response quality may have comparatively limited influence.

The theoretical analysis characterizes DPO’s optimal response distribution and examines why contrast between responses helps. It finds that contrastiveness contributes primarily through improving the chosen samples. In an online DPO setting studied by the authors, the method effectively reduces to supervised fine-tuning on chosen responses, further emphasizing their role.

Experiments across diverse tasks consistently show benefits from improving chosen responses regardless of rejected-response quality. The paper also investigates mixing in on-policy data. Together, the findings suggest prioritizing the quality of preferred examples when constructing preference datasets. They explain mechanisms behind existing data strategies while preserving the distinction between a dominant contribution from chosen responses and the more limited role that rejected responses may play.
neurips-2025-what-matters-in-data-for-dp.tldr: Theory and experiments identify chosen-response quality as the dominant driver of DPO performance, with rejected-response quality potentially less influential.
